site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: A Bowl of Rice, A Half of Kingdom
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. III, Maha-assaroha Jataka (No. 302) — E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: Driven from his throne, a king wandered starving through a dusty village until a poor farmer opened his door. Recognising the royal face beneath the traveler's dust, he welcomed the fugitive and shared with him the single meal meant for his own wife and children, asking nothing in return.

When the king at last reclaimed his kingdom, he did not forget the humble hearth that had sheltered him. He summoned the farmer to court, placed half the realm into those calloused hands, and raised the farmer's sons to seats on the council of ministers.
Whispers moved through the palace that evening, soft as temple bells at dusk. A single bowl of rice, received with quiet gratitude, had grown into the greatest honour the crown could bestow.

stories.title: King Sibi on the Scale of Mercy
stories.source: Mahabharata · Vana Parva, Tirtha-yatra Parva (Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation)
body: During his great Rajasuya sacrifice, King Sibi of Ausala looked down to find a trembling dove fallen into his lap, a falcon hard behind it. He folded his hands and called the dove his guest, refusing to surrender a life that had sought his shelter. Even when the falcon answered that he, too, must eat, the king would not turn away.

Sibi agreed to the strange exchange the falcon proposed: flesh cut from his own body, weighed against the small feathered creature. Piece by piece his own flesh went on the scale, yet somehow the dove grew heavier. Without flinching, Sibi climbed onto the pan himself, offering his whole being for the bird he had promised to protect.

At that, the falcon and the dove shone with heavenly light, revealing themselves as Agni, Dharma, and the king of birds. The gods smiled upon Sibi, blessed him for his unwavering compassion, and gently healed every wound. In the quiet after the miracle, the hall of the sacrifice glowed with grace.

stories.title: The King Whose Jasmine Found the Himalayas
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. III, Aditta-Jataka (No. 424), E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: In the kingdom of Sovira, King Bharata grieved that his alms-hall fed the undeserving. With his wise queen Samuddavijaya, he filled a gold box with jasmine flowers and saluted the four quarters, casting seven handfuls into the northern sky.

The blossoms rose above the world and floated gently onto five hundred Paccekabuddhas gathered in the Nandamula cave of the Himalayas. Seven of these awakened ones drifted back through the air and descended to the palace gate, where the king and queen welcomed them with humble hands.

For seven days they shared the kingdom's finest food, then offered robes and bowls as gifts. Sovira flourished, and the discerning generosity of Bharata and Samuddavijaya was praised throughout the land as a light that had reached the mountains.

stories.title: The Brave Guardian Mongoose
stories.source: Panchatantra · Tantra 4 (Vira Mitra / 'Loss of Friends'), 'The Brahmin and the Mongoose', Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: By the dusty roadside, a gentle brahmin raised a tiny mongoose as one of his own, trusting the bright-eyed creature to watch over his humble home. The mongoose grew into a faithful guardian, patrolling the doorway with quiet devotion and warming himself by the family's clay lamp each evening.

One afternoon, as the mother bathed, she laid their infant son in the cradle and asked the mongoose to keep watch. A black cobra slithered toward the child, but the mongoose leapt upon it and tore it apart, his muzzle reddened when the mother stepped from the water and saw only blood on his face.

Seized by fear, she struck him down with her water-pot. When the brahmin returned, he found his son unharmed beside the slain serpent, and mourned the loyal friend lost to a hasty heart. Yet the child's safe smile remained, a small mercy glowing through the sorrow.

stories.title: Flowers for the Virtuous Heart
stories.source: The Jataka · Vol. V, Kurudhamma Jataka (No. 276), E. B. Cowell ed., public domain
body: In Indapatta, King Koravya of the Yuddhitthila line longed to offer his gifts only to those truly worthy. His counsellor Vidhura, the wise Bodhisatta, gently taught him the marks of a real brahmin: a soul free from selfishness, deceit, and the pull of the senses.

When the king asked where such sages could be found, Vidhura pointed toward the further Himalaya and a quiet cave on Mount Nanda. He cast eight handfuls of flowers into the air, and five hundred Paccekabuddhas received them, descending to the palace.

For seven days the king honoured them with food, robes, and the requisites of a simple life. Then, their cups of merit full, the awakened ones rose together through the roof, leaving the whole court wrapped in a calm and lasting joy.
